demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
**Patient Name:** "David" (pseudonym)
**Age:** 34
**Occupation:** School Counselor
**Trauma:** Accidentally caused serious injury to a student during a lockdown drill

David is a tall, soft-spoken man who often looks down at his hands when he speaks. He has been married for eight years and has two young children, ages four and six. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, after she found him standing in the garage at 3 a.m., staring at the family car.

The event happened eight months ago, during a routine active shooter drill at the middle school where he works. David was responsible for locking down the east wing. He remembers the intercom crackling, the sound of his own heartbeat, the heavy door slamming shut. But what he cannot forget is the moment he saw Mateo, a seventh grader with a quiet smile, running toward the door from the wrong side of the hall. David’s hand moved before his brain could catch up. He shoved the door closed, hard. He did not see Mateo’s fingers curl around the jamb.

The sound was something between a wet snap and a scream. Mateo’s hand was crushed in the doorframe. Three fingers were broken so badly that one required surgical pinning. David remembers kneeling beside the boy, his own hands shaking as he tried to hold the boy’s wrist, the blood pooling on the linoleum. He remembers saying, *“I’m sorry, I’m so sorry,”* over and over, while a teacher pulled him away.

In the weeks that followed, David told himself it was an accident. He told his wife the same thing. He went back to work. He smiled at students in the hallway. He attended a meeting about improving drill protocols. But inside, something had cracked. He began to avoid the east wing entirely, taking a longer route to his office. He stopped eating lunch in the staff lounge because someone might ask about it. He started scanning hallways for kids who ran, for hands near doors.

The nightmares started about a month in. They are not violent in the way one might expect. In the dreams, David is always running toward Mateo, but the hallway stretches endlessly. He can see the boy’s face, but when he reaches him, Mateo’s hands are fine—perfect, whole. And then David looks down at his own hands, and they are covered in blood. He wakes up gasping, his heart slamming against his ribs, his wife’s hand on his shoulder. He has not slept through the night since.

His work has become a minefield. As a school counselor, David is trained to sit with distress, to listen, to hold space for pain. But now, when a student cries in his office, he feels a surge of panic. He finds himself clenching his jaw, his palms slick with sweat. He has started to dread the sound of a door closing. Any door. The soft click of his office door, the heavy slam of a car door, the bathroom stall door at the grocery store. He flinches every time.

His wife, Sarah, has noticed the changes. He is irritable with the children. He snapped at his six-year-old for slamming the refrigerator door. He has stopped driving the family to school because the sight of kids running toward the building makes his vision blur. He has lost twelve pounds. He drinks three cups of coffee by 9 a.m. just to feel awake, but his mind is always half-elsewhere, scanning, waiting.

He scored a 77 on the PCL-5 during the intake. He did not ask what it meant. He just nodded, looked at his hands, and said, *“I used to think I was good at helping people.”*
